strengths: Well-motivated practical problem domain (500M Excel users) with clear societal relevance and understudied status

Comprehensive, multi-layered evaluation framework integrating programmatic features (29 well-defined metrics), data-driven failure taxonomy (validated 78% with experts), and domain-expert evaluation—providing valuable triangulation
Methodologically rigorous: proper application of Bradley-Terry model with feature augmentation, appropriate causal disclaimers, thorough feature significance testing across domains
Important empirical finding that crowd preferences diverge from professional financial standards (42.3% expert-crowd agreement), with clear implications for RLHF-based post-training
Exceptional reproducibility: comprehensive appendices with system prompts, JSON schema, 29 feature definitions, model configs, failure taxonomy, evaluation rubrics; promised dataset release
Novel combination of techniques in new domain: Arena evaluation + feature decomposition + failure taxonomy applied to end-to-end spreadsheet generation at scale (4,357 votes, 16 models)

Multi-domain insights: Dramatic domain-specific ranking shifts (Claude 1st→9th in Academic domain) reveal that evaluation criteria fundamentally vary by use case, supporting use-case-dependent preference modeling
Live platform and dataset provide lasting community value beyond the paper's immediate findings
weaknesses: Expert-crowd disagreement (42.3% overall, 56.4% for decisive cases) is documented but not deeply explained—paper fails to analyze why professionals and crowds value different attributes, limiting insights for future work

Low inter-rater reliability in expert study (Krippendorff's α: 0.27–0.51) undermines confidence in the expert ground truth and raises questions about whether 'professional standards' are contested even among domain experts

Concerning feature effects: Formula sophistication (lookups, conditionals, constants) shows no significant association with preferences while presentation features (text density +1.56, fills +1.15) dominate—suggests preference signals reward style over substance, but paper doesn't explore why or propose mitigation

Limited actionability: Paper provides rankings and feature analysis but minimal guidance on how to improve spreadsheet generation; vague references to 'upstream interventions' and 'data curation' without concrete proposals
Task formulation constraints: Assumes single end-to-end JSON generation, excluding iterative/agentic approaches that professionals commonly use; limits generalizability of findings

Failure taxonomy validation uses circular pipeline (GPT-5-mini generates rationales → cluster → hand-curate → validate on 50 samples), risking bias toward LLM-derived failure categories; no independent expert categorization

Insufficient analysis of dramatic domain-specific reversals (e.g., Academic & Research rankings completely shuffle); explanation of number formatting coefficient (-5.38) is plausible but under-explored
Low inter-rater agreement in expert study combined with small sample (15 triply-rated, 89 single-rated) limits confidence in reliability dimension of expert evaluation

Missing important experimental details: Arena URL blank in paper; prompt complexity distribution not provided; vote distribution per prompt/model pair unclear; no analysis of systematic model disagreements
Primarily a dataset/evaluation paper with limited algorithmic innovation; doesn't advance spreadsheet generation methods themselves, only characterizes what exists

strengths: Addresses important understudied domain: spreadsheet generation affects ~500M users but receives minimal research attention compared to code generation

Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation combining arena votes (4,357), programmatic feature analysis (29 features), data-driven failure taxonomy, and domain expert evaluation—more thorough than typical single-metric evaluations
Excellent experimental rigor: proper blinding, Benjamini-Hochberg corrections, feature-augmented Bradley-Terry model that cleanly decomposes preference sources, and fully-crossed expert design

Rich nuanced findings revealing domain-specificity: feature effects vary dramatically across categories (p < 10⁻⁶⁸), model families exhibit distinct failure signatures (e.g., Claude loses on correctness while others lose on presentation), and features like finance_color_convention are significant only within domain
Feature adjustment reveals substantial confounding: leaderboard compression from 918 Elo to 550 points shows formatting/structure features bias raw rankings, validating need for decomposition
High-quality reporting: extensive appendices with complete methodology, SheetSpec specification, evaluator instructions, example spreadsheets, and detailed failure taxonomy definitions
Practical contribution: live platform, dataset release (1,033 prompts + 4,357 votes), and code release promise to support future research
weaknesses: Critical validity concern: expert-arena agreement is only 56.0% (63.6% for decisive comparisons), barely above chance, with low inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's α = 0.28-0.45). This raises fundamental questions about whether crowd votes reflect genuine quality versus preference bias (formatting, verbosity). Paper acknowledges but doesn't investigate causes or implications

No training/improvement experiments: paper claims findings 'have implications for post-training' (p.3) but provides no RLHF or finetuning experiments validating this. Without demonstrating that insights improve models, practical impact is limited to infrastructure

Limited methodological novelty: Bradley-Terry models (Bradley & Terry 1952), feature-augmented BT adapts Scale AI (2025), arena evaluation from Chiang et al. (2024), failure taxonomy methodology from Deng et al. (2025). Primarily applies existing techniques to new domain rather than developing novel methods

Formula sophistication features show no significant effects (lookup p=0.73, conditionals p=0.28, constants p=0.55) despite being central to generation tasks. This surprising null result lacks investigation—unclear whether it reflects crowdworker inability to evaluate correctness, prompts not emphasizing it, or formatting overwhelming evaluation

Expert evaluation severely limited in scope and reliability: only 25 finance battles (vs. 500+ prompts), low inter-rater reliability undermines confidence, overall expert rating 2.86/5 with only 16.1% circulation-worthy. Missing analysis of whether gap reflects models' fundamental incapability or evaluation miscalibration

Voter identity unspecified: paper doesn't disclose arena voter demographics or expertise (crowdworkers vs. researchers vs. domain specialists), yet this substantially affects interpretation. Chiang et al. (2024) specified 'community voters,' but this paper doesn't

Feature interpretation conflates correlation with quality: text density (+1.56), fills (+1.15), numeric content (+1.02) are strongest predictors. Unclear if this captures genuine quality or mirrors 'length bias' seen in dialogue evaluation (Hu et al. 2025)—needs analysis of actual user utility

Presentation issues: paper attempts to cover too much (rankings, features, failures, expert eval), making some sections rushed. Critical finding (expert-crowd misalignment 56%) mentioned in passing. Domain-specific feature variation (§5.2.2) deserves more prominence—this is a key insight
